title: Line in three ranging rods between two fixed poles, with no line drawn
instruction: Stand the three red rods upright on the table between the two yellow poles so that all five are in one straight line, with every gap between neighbouring rods or poles along the line at least 7 cm and at most 16 cm.
context: Surveying and construction crews line in intermediate ranging rods or stakes between two fixed control points so that a boundary, fence or set-out line runs straight; nothing is marked on the ground between the points. The robot has to place three points on an unmarked 45 cm line defined only by two distant references at its ends, keeping all three on it and spaced along it, rather than extending a line from one reference or following a drawn one.
setup: World frame for this text: 'in front' is away from the arm bases, 'left' and 'right' are from the robot's view, heights are above the table top, and the midline is halfway between the two arm bases (the bases are 61.0 cm apart). Nothing is drawn on the table along or near the line between the poles (on a real rig, small tape marks at the rods' start spots, well away from the line, are fine for resetting). Fixed poles: two yellow painted-steel cylinders, 16 mm in diameter and 150 mm tall, standing on the table and fixed to it. Pole A is centred 20.0 cm in front of the arm bases and 20.0 cm left of the midline; pole B is centred 40.0 cm in front and 20.0 cm right of the midline. Their centres are 447.2 mm apart. Loose rods: three identical red plastic cylinders, 24 mm in diameter and 100 mm tall, 40 g each, standing upright on the table, all centred 14.0 cm in front of the arm bases: rod 1 at 13.0 cm left of the midline, rod 2 at 5.0 cm left and rod 3 at 9.0 cm right. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial, after the arms have withdrawn (the simulator cannot see the gripper, so in simulation a rod held still with its bottom on the table also counts as standing). The line runs through the centres of the two poles. To lay it out with a string, stretch the string tangent to the same side of both poles: because the poles are the same size it runs parallel to the line, 8 mm from it. A rod counts as standing when it is upright on either end, its axis within 5 degrees of vertical, its top at least 90 mm above its bottom, its bottom is within 1 mm of the table top, and it is at rest (moving under 1 cm/s and turning under 0.5 rad/s). For each rod measure its offset, the distance from its centre (its axis) to the line at right angles, and its station, how far along the line from pole A's centre the foot of that right angle falls. Hard rules: all three rods standing; every station strictly between 0 and 447.2 mm (between the poles, not beyond either); and, taking pole A, the three rods in order along the line, and pole B, each of the four gaps between neighbours along the line from 70 to 160 mm inclusive. If any hard rule fails the score is 0. Otherwise the worst rod's offset sets the score: at most 5 mm, 1.0; at most 10 mm, 0.6; at most 20 mm, 0.3; over 20 mm, 0. Every outcome is covered: a rod lying down, tilted more than 5 degrees, standing on another rod, held above the table, left at its start, beyond a pole or crowding another rod or a pole (a gap under 70 mm) scores 0 for the trial, as do the rods bunched together so an end gap exceeds 160 mm. The rods are identical, so which rod goes where does not matter. Success, which ends the trial early, is the 1.0 condition holding for 1 s. The start scores 0 (all three rods are off the line).
reset_notes: Stand the three rods back on their start spots (14.0 cm in front of the arm bases at 13.0 cm and 5.0 cm left and 9.0 cm right of the midline; small tape marks there make this quick). The poles do not move. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Approximate. Poles and rods are rigid cylinders; a real ranging rod is about 2 m tall with red and white bands, and lining in is done by eye over tens of metres, not across a table. In simulation the poles are fixed to the table; on a real rig they would be clamped or glued. The scorer reads each rod's centre and tilt from the simulator; on a real rig the same quantities are measured with a string, a ruler and a tape. Friction and mass are the simulator's values for these shapes, not measured.
